claims.text: High-entropy alloys contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The initial nanoparticles are simple, chemically disordered, single-phase solid solutions.
Maintenance of a single-phase solid solution across 473–1923 K is governed by the degree of lattice distortion.
Differences in constituent atomic radii induce lattice distortion.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch while retaining near-equiatomic composition increases lattice distortion.
Local strain fields produced by lattice distortion suppress atomic diffusion.
Enhanced lattice distortion increases the kinetic barrier for atomic diffusion.
Slower diffusion reduces atomic rearrangements that cause phase segregation and chemical inhomogeneity.
High configurational entropy lowers the free energy of simple solid-solution phases, particularly at high temperature.
High configurational entropy makes chemically ordered intermetallic compounds less competitive.
Diffusion suppression from lattice distortion enables configurational entropy to preserve the solid solution during severe thermal cycling.
Higher-distortion nanoparticles will retain a single-phase, chemically uniform structure better than lower-mismatch controls.
Higher-distortion nanoparticles will exhibit less phase separation and chemical segregation than the initial lower-mismatch baseline after thermal exposure.
Lower-atomic-size-mismatch control nanoparticles may undergo phase separation or chemical inhomogeneity under the specified thermal conditions.
The comparison will hold atmosphere, support, synthesis route, and other processing parameters constant while varying atomic-size mismatch.
The proposed relationship applies over catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions spanning 473–1923 K.
Excessive atomic-size differences can make enthalpic interactions favor intermetallic-compound formation over a single-phase solid solution.
The mechanism is expected to apply only while the alloy remains within a single-phase solid-solution regime.
Long-term catalytic or thermoelectric performance can serve as an indirect probe of structural stability.
Failure of the higher-distortion particles to outperform the control in single-phase retention or chemical homogeneity would falsify the hypothesis.
